article: How is social jet lag calculated from your sleep times?
Use a worked example to compare sleep midpoints on workdays and free days.
Wittmann and colleagues’ original research on social jetlag. Schedule example is invented and illustrative.
related: See how to keep a sleep diary
copy: Social jet lag is often expressed as the difference between the midpoint of sleep on workdays and on free days. If you sleep from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. on workdays and 1 a.m. to 9 a.m. on free days, both spells last eight hours. Their midpoints differ by two hours.
Use clock time around midnight consistently

Find the halfway point from estimated sleep onset to waking. For a midnight-crossing interval, count elapsed time first so the date change does not produce a negative number. Some studies adjust the calculation to account for differences in sleep duration, so note which form a paper uses.
The result describes timing in this example. It does not diagnose a sleep problem.

article: Can you feel used to short sleep while reaction times still get worse?
Compare the self-report and task outcomes in a controlled multi-night sleep restriction study.
Van Dongen et al. controlled human sleep restriction study with objective and subjective outcomes.
copy: A laboratory experiment found that reduced time in bed could produce cumulative problems on attention tasks. How sleepy participants said they felt did not track the accumulating performance change in the same way. Each outcome answers a different question.
Read the accumulated task effect separately

The researchers assigned different nightly opportunities for sleep and repeatedly tested people over many days. A participant can grow accustomed to a feeling even when task lapses continue changing. This is a group observation under assigned conditions, rather than a way to infer an individual’s alertness from a schedule.
A phone reaction test or a sleepiness score cannot certify that you are safe to drive or operate equipment.

article: Can an older-adult bedroom study tell you the best sleep temperature for everyone?
Read the temperature and sleep measurements separately before treating a fitted association as a universal setting.
Baniassadi et al. observational home study of community-dwelling older adults.
related: See how to keep a sleep diary
copy: A home study of older adults related nighttime bedroom temperature to wearable-derived sleep measures. The relationship was not identical across participants. That study offers more direct evidence about their bedrooms than a distant weather measurement, but it does not set one temperature for everyone.
Check how the temperature was observed

The researchers observed real living conditions instead of randomly assigning thermostat settings. Bedding, building conditions and individual circumstances can matter alongside room temperature. A fitted range in a group analysis is not the same as a personal threshold.
When sharing the result, name the age group, note that it was an observational study, and keep the measured bedroom temperature distinct from the thermostat display.

article: Does having a light on while sleeping test the same thing as using a screen before bed?
Distinguish exposure during a sleep period from evening reading using two controlled studies.
Mason et al. light-during-sleep study and Chang et al. evening light-emitting reader study.
copy: A room-light experiment measured exposure during the sleep period. The e-reader experiment gave people reading conditions before sleep. Both involve light, but the timing and outcomes differ. You cannot use the results interchangeably just because a headline says night light.
Put the exposure on a timeline

Find the exposure start and end relative to bedtime. Mason’s study assessed heart and metabolic measures after a defined overnight condition. Chang’s study examined circadian timing and other sleep-related outcomes after pre-bed reading. Keep light at the point of measurement, the comparison lighting and the specific outcome visible.
A dim phone before bedtime and a lit room during sleep are different interventions. Look for a study that tested the question you intend to answer.

article: Why might two e-reader sleep experiments find different results?
Compare two original reader studies by exposure timing and background daytime light.
Two original controlled studies comparing light-emitting readers with physical books, with different protocols.
copy: One controlled study reported changes in sleep and circadian outcomes after evening light-emitting e-reader use. A different experiment had participants receive daytime bright light and tested two hours of evening reading on a tablet or a physical book. It did not find the same changes in its conditions.
Look beyond the type of screen

The studies vary in the devices, exposure schedules and background light. That leaves more than one plausible reason for different results. The later experiment does not isolate daytime light as the only reason the studies differ. Read the actual timing and surrounding conditions rather than drawing one conclusion for every screen.
Check whether the claim refers to melatonin, falling asleep or next-day alertness. The outcomes are separate even within a single experiment.

article: Does an evening workout sleep study measure when you finished or how hard you exercised?
Read a large wearable analysis by time and exercise strain, and keep its observational design visible.
Original real-world wearable cohort study on evening exercise strain and sleep timing.
related: See how to keep a sleep diary
copy: A large wearable study considered both exercise timing and the recorded strain of a session. A walk and a hard interval workout that end at the same time can occupy different places in that analysis. Clock time alone is not the exposure being modeled.
Use time and strain as separate variables

The researchers observed what people actually did and estimated their sleep from wearable records. That design can show patterns over many nights. It cannot guarantee what would happen if a particular person changed only the hour of a workout. Work and meal timing can go along with exercise timing.
When reading a headline, check the sleep outcome and the interval from the end of the exercise session to the actual sleep time.

article: What did a weekend catch-up sleep experiment actually test?
Compare assigned weeknight sleep, weekend recovery and the repeating schedule in an original lab trial.
Depner et al. controlled human study of recurring sleep restriction with or without a weekend recovery opportunity.
copy: The trial did not just ask whether people could sleep longer over a weekend. It tested a recurring pattern of restricted sleep, an opportunity for weekend recovery and then another period of restriction. Some metabolic changes persisted or reappeared under the repeating schedule.
Follow the measurements into the next week

A result measured during the recovery window can look different from one measured after participants return to the restricted schedule. Keep those time points separate. An average from short laboratory observations also cannot quantify the long-term health effect of a person’s usual weekend routine.
Look up the specific endpoint before repeating a claim that a weekend erased all consequences of short sleep.

article: How did a sleep-extension trial estimate food intake without counting each meal?
Follow the two measurements that researchers used to estimate energy intake in a real-life sleep study.
Tasali et al. randomized study of 80 adults with overweight and habitual short sleep. Energy intake estimated from energy balance.
copy: The researchers combined estimated energy expenditure with changes in the body’s energy stores. That gives an estimate of how much energy participants took in over the measurement window. It does not identify specific meals or tell you which foods changed.
Separate estimated intake from a diary

The randomized comparison involved adults who usually slept less than 6.5 hours and met the study’s eligibility criteria. The sleep-extension group’s average estimated intake fell by about 270 kcal per day compared with the control group over the short intervention. That group estimate cannot be turned into a fixed calorie effect for every extra hour of someone’s sleep.
The result concerns an average and a specific study population. It does not identify a personal food target.

article: Can a short-sleep experiment measure hunger without measuring what people ate?
Distinguish appetite ratings and hormone measurements from free-choice intake.
Spiegel et al. controlled short-duration human sleep manipulation with hormone and appetite outcomes.
copy: An early experiment compared hormone measurements and self-reported hunger after assigned sleep conditions in a small group of healthy young men. It observed a change in appetite-related measures. Those readouts do not by themselves measure how much food people freely chose to eat.
Look for an intake outcome before quoting calories

A hormone value, a hunger rating and a weighed meal all cover different parts of the question. If sellers claim a numeric difference in calories, look for a study that actually recorded or estimated intake. A small, short experiment may identify a mechanism worth testing without answering what happens over months.
Check the sample and feeding conditions as well as sleep duration. They matter when comparing it with a study in ordinary life.

article: Can the same reported overnight noise level produce different awakenings?
Compare event-based and average measurements in an original traffic-noise sleep study.
Original sleep lab and field studies on air, road or rail traffic noise and polysomnography.
related: See how to keep a sleep diary
copy: An overnight average combines quiet intervals and louder events. That average does not tell you when a train passed, how loud it was in the room or whether an awakening followed it. Traffic-noise researchers used event timing and recorded sleep to examine those questions.
Check events as well as the nightly summary

A laboratory comparison can control the timing and sound recordings. A field study observes the sound people actually encounter at home, where buildings and other noise sources differ. The frequency and pattern of events can help explain why matching one summary number does not reproduce every sleep effect.
Keep the source of the noise and the measured sleep outcome with the result before applying it to a specific room.

article: Did a sleep-onset warming experiment heat the bedroom or the skin?
Check the body site and measurement in controlled warming research.
Original human cutaneous warming and skin-temperature sleep-onset studies. This is study interpretation.
copy: In the original warming research, investigators controlled temperature at particular skin locations and tracked sleep onset. This is different from turning up the whole room overnight. The exposed area, timing and measured outcome belong in any claim about what changed.
Match the intervention to the headline

Sleep-onset latency describes how long it took to fall asleep under the study conditions. That value says little about later awakenings, the next day or room-temperature preferences. Age and other participant differences also matter when comparing studies with different samples.
If a headline recommends a room setting using this paper, check whether that room setting was an experimental condition. The original result directly concerns its defined skin exposure.

article: Why can exercise-heat studies disagree when they use different thermometers?
Read how researchers checked field devices against a reference measure during exercise.
Original device validation studies during outdoor exercise or under wind and sweat conditions.
copy: A thermometer can respond to the environment around the point it measures. Research comparing field devices found that readings at different sites could diverge during exercise in the heat. An oral or skin measure does not automatically stand in for a measurement used as a core-temperature reference.
Compare the device under the same conditions

Look at the agreement for individuals and how it changed under wind or sweating. Two methods can have similar averages and still disagree for an individual at a particular time. A temperature difference in a recovery study may reflect both physiology and the method used to record it.
These papers validate measurement methods. They are not instructions for evaluating a heat emergency.
